stats.howRatingWorks.title: How rating and CS Rating are calculated
stats.howRatingWorks.subtitle: every term, every default
stats.howRatingWorks.ratingDesc1: A round is scored against what an average round looks like here. Each of the five parts is your value divided by the expected value, so 1.00 is average and 2.00 is twice it. The parts are then weighted and added:
stats.howRatingWorks.ratingDesc2: The weights sum to 1.00, which is what keeps an average round at 1.00 rather than some arbitrary number. A season's rating is the mean of its rounds, clamped to
stats.howRatingWorks.averageDesc: Kills and damage expectations scale with how many enemies are actually alive, so a 3v3 is not judged against 5v5 numbers. Round type shifts them too: pistol rounds expect slightly less, full buys slightly more.
stats.howRatingWorks.impactDesc: Impact is the part that is not visible in a scoreboard. It is a sum of events:
stats.howRatingWorks.plantingHeading: Why planting and defusing are worth nothing
stats.howRatingWorks.plantingDesc1: This is a retake server. The bomb is
stats.howRatingWorks.plantingDesc2: when the round starts, and the CTs have to defuse it to win — so both were paying you for doing the thing the round is about. Everyone who played competently collected them every round, which made them a measure of attendance rather than contribution. They are set to zero rather than removed, so an older season's numbers still reproduce exactly.
stats.howRatingWorks.tkHeading: Why a team kill can be worth a little
stats.howRatingWorks.tkDesc: Killing a teammate while the round is live costs your team the round, and is penalised. Once every enemy is dead or the bomb is already defused, nothing is at stake — so it is a joke rather than a throw. It pays a small amount: enough to be worth something, never enough to be worth farming.
stats.howRatingWorks.csRatingDesc: Elo moves on whether your team won the round, adjusted by how likely that was and by how well you personally played. The expectation comes from the two teams' average ratings:
stats.howRatingWorks.eloDesc1: K sets how fast ratings move; the divisor of 400 is the standard Elo scale, meaning a 400-point gap makes you roughly ten times more likely to win.
stats.howRatingWorks.eloDesc2: The performance factor is your round rating, so winning while playing badly gains less than winning while carrying, and losing while playing well costs less.
stats.howRatingWorks.eloBounds3: . Rounds you were AFK for are excluded entirely.
stats.howRatingWorks.seasonDesc: These values are fixed per season. A change made for a coming season is written against that season and does nothing until it starts — so no round is ever re-priced after it was played, and the rating you were shown at the time stays the rating you earned.
stats.howRatingWorks.s2Desc: Everything above still runs. Season 2 adds two new sources of points, changes how far one session can move you, and stops the ladder dead for the three days a season takes to end.
stats.howRatingWorks.s2Note: Where a coefficient below is written as a name — kUp, wSelf, kSteady — the server has not fixed that number yet. The shape of each formula is settled and is published here; the constants are published on this page the day Season 2 opens. A made-up number set in the same typeface as a real one would make this whole page worthless.
stats.howRatingWorks.swingHeading: CS Rating moves further, and further down
stats.howRatingWorks.swingDesc1: The K factor is split in two. A session that gains you rating is multiplied by one number, a session that loses it by a larger one, and both are bigger than the single K Season 1 used.
stats.howRatingWorks.swingDesc2: Season 1's ladder stopped moving around February. The players at the top had banked a lead no ordinary bad month could spend, so the order stopped answering the only question anyone asks a ladder — who is playing well now. A rating that only ratchets upward is a join date. Moving faster in both directions means a good night is worth staying up for, a bad one is worth quitting before, and the top ten in week twenty is the top ten of week twenty.
stats.howRatingWorks.mapDesc1: Every map you play is now scored twice: against your own average across all maps, and against what the whole server averages on that map. Both comparisons feed the same pot of points.
stats.howRatingWorks.mapDesc2: Both halves have to be there. Measured only against yourself, a player who is weak everywhere farms the bonus by being slightly less weak than usual; measured only against the server, the map bonus is just the rating you already earned, paid a second time.
stats.howRatingWorks.mapWhy: Rating already knew you had a good round. It did not know that you have good rounds on Nuke and bad ones on Ancient, and it paid the same for both. Beating your own Ancient by a clear margin is a real result even when the raw numbers are worse than your worst Nuke, and Season 2 pays for it.
stats.howRatingWorks.dailyDesc1b: Paris time the server reads back every ranked round you played the day before and scores how alike they were. It is a pass of its own, run once, over a day that has finished — consistency is a property of a whole night and cannot be known while the night is still being played.
stats.howRatingWorks.dailyDesc2: It is measured against you, not against the ladder. Ten rounds at 0.80 score better than five at 1.60 and five at 0.10, even though the second player had the bigger night and the better average. A retake server is a queue of strangers who get four seconds to decide who takes which angle: the player everyone can plan around is worth more to that queue than the one who is unplayable four rounds in five.
stats.howRatingWorks.dailyDesc3: This is also why a consistent bad day still pays. Playing badly the same way every round is a fixable problem — it has one cause, someone can name it, and you can go and practise it. Playing well and badly at random is not information about anything, least of all to the four people counting on you.
stats.howRatingWorks.dailyMultiplier: What the pass produces is not points but a multiplier on your next session's Elo movement. The multiplier persists until your next session — taking a break doesn't reset your consistency streak. It holds while you keep the run going and fades back toward 1.00 as soon as you stop, so it can never be banked: the bonus belongs to the streak, not to the account, and the day you stop being predictable is the day you stop being paid for it.
stats.howRatingWorks.globalDesc: Alongside the daily pass, the season keeps one consistency figure across every ranked day you have played, and it feeds the same multiplier at a smaller weight. It moves slowly on purpose: one blown Saturday should not undo three months of showing up, and one brilliant Saturday should not buy them.
stats.howRatingWorks.freezeDesc1: A season now ends the moment its community vote opens. For the
stats.howRatingWorks.freezeDesc1b: hours the ballot is up, no round moves anyone's CS Rating. Rounds still count for stats, clips and medals; Elo alone is frozen, until the next season starts.
stats.howRatingWorks.freezeDesc2: The vote hands out awards for a season that has already happened, and a ladder still moving underneath the ballot invites the closing-night rush — three hours of stacking to land a place in a category before the polls shut. Freezing the number takes the prize off the table and leaves the last three days as rounds people play because they want to.

loadout.role.sniper.desc: Holds the long angle and opens the site from range.
loadout.role.lurker.desc: Plays alone to cut off rotations and catch the flank.
loadout.role.rifler.desc: First through the smoke. Trades space for information.
loadout.role.entry.desc: First through the smoke. Trades space for information.
loadout.role.support.desc: Throws the utility that gets the entry in.
loadout.role.trade.desc: Second man. Punishes whoever takes the entry.
loadout.role.awp.desc: Holds the long angle and opens the site from range.
loadout.role.anchor.desc: Holds the bomb and plays for the timer.
loadout.role.rotator.desc: Plays off the anchor and arrives from the flank.
loadout.role.flex.desc: Takes whatever the other four did not.
loadout.role.sniper.retake.T: The site's long angle, and the one gun on it nobody can replace. You hold the corridor the retake has to cross and take its first shot — everything your team does afterwards is built on whether that shot lands. You are not part of the site hold; you are why they have to walk into it slowly.
loadout.role.sniper.retake.CT: You open the retake from outside the site, before anybody walks in. One angle, one shot, then move — a retake that stands still waiting for the AWP to find a second kill is a retake that runs out of clock.
loadout.role.lurker.retake.T: You are not on the site. You sit behind the retake, let it commit, and take it from the back — the second wave and the flank are yours. Dying early costs your team the only player who can see the retake from behind it.
loadout.role.rifler.retake.T: On the site, on the bomb. You hold the plant, trade whoever they kill first, and make the clock the CTs' problem instead of yours. A retake usually wants more than one of you, which is why this one is not capped.
loadout.role.anchor.retake.CT: First body onto the site. You take the space the bomb is in, and the whole retake is timed off your entry — the job is not to win the round alone, it is to be inside and alive long enough for the defuse to start.
loadout.role.rotator.retake.CT: You come in second, from the other entrance, a beat after the anchor. Your job is the trade: whoever kills them is looking the wrong way when you arrive. More than one rotator is normal — a retake from one direction is not a retake.
